Those sanctioned can now file an appeal to the UN via an ombudsperson. Appointed by the UN Secretary General in consultation with the committee, the ombudsperson is essentially a mediator for a process that occurs outside a court. They request information from member states and conduct independent research, then interview the petitioner and others. It can take up to sixteen months for them to issue a report and recommendation, which the committee has to vote unanimously to accept.

Complicating the process further is the fact that the US can recommend sanctions based purely on intelligence information, while European countries do so only if there has been a criminal investigation. Sometimes the ombudsperson can access the initial intelligence from the listing state; other times they’re denied on national security grounds. Some of the Security Council committee members—the five permanent seats are Russia, China, the US, the UK, and France—refuse to exchange information with one another. Even less gets shared with the people on the list, and therefore with their legal counsel. Although the “reasons for listing” are given, this is often only a short statement of allegations. “The basis upon which the listing happens is in the shadow world of information, and the shadow world of intelligence agencies and cooperation between states,” Ní Aoláin has said.

Only a handful of lawyers are willing to navigate these peculiar procedures. Among them is an Edinburgh-based solicitor and legal scholar named Gavin Sullivan. An Australian-British citizen with a tangled mop of dark hair and professorial spectacles, Sullivan tends to work overtime on cases others avoid. In 2010 he was on staff at a human rights organization in Berlin when a migrants’ association in France contacted him. He scanned the email: a number of Tunisian immigrants in France had wound up on the UN al-Qaeda list, one of whom lost his bricklaying business, pushing his family, including four young children, into poverty. Sullivan was himself the son of a bricklayer and the first in his family to attend university; it made no sense to him that a Tunisian builder could end up on an international blacklist alongside men like bin Laden.

He took the man’s case, along with those of four others, and soon discovered how difficult it was to argue against secret evidence and unsubstantiated allegations. “You’re trying to defend someone, but you don’t know from what,” Sullivan told me. “It’s like shooting in the dark.” Eventually Sullivan got all five off the list, with the help of colleagues including the barrister Rachel Barnes and the Italian legal academic Alice Riccardi. But the requests for his assistance kept coming. One of his clients had been listed for more than fifteen years; for another case, Sullivan received a scant two paragraphs of information. Since that initial case, all six of the clients he has represented have been delisted. Overall, nearly 70 percent of delisting petitions are granted, indicating that a high number of people are mistakenly included in the first place.

In January 2016 Sullivan moved to the University of Kent, where he started teaching law. The UN does not provide legal aid to people trying to challenge the blacklist. Sullivan—who believes that everyone should be entitled to an adequate legal defense, especially during proceedings that rely on secret evidence—has had to carve out time around his day job, relying on volunteer translators to parse redaction-heavy case documents in multiple languages. While raising two young daughters, he started writing a book about the global listing architecture.

In late 2017 Sullivan and Barnes were contacted by Baraa Shiban, a well-known leader of the Arab Spring in Yemen who had fled the country in 2015, after the Houthis began abducting journalists, activists, and members of civil society. Now in London, Shiban asked the lawyers if they’d take on a new case: that of a bright Yemeni leader whose life had been derailed by the UN blacklist.

2.

While the Arab Spring unfurled in Sanaa in 2011, Naif, then twenty-eight, was glued to the TV coverage from his home in Saudi Arabia. Born into a semi-prominent family in Al-Bayda, where tribes are an important form of social organization, Naif grew up hearing stories about the bravery of his father, Salih Salem al-Qaysi, a community leader who was murdered by bandits during a roadside ambush when Naif was five. This impressed upon him how important it was for the state to give its citizens basic security.

At university in Sanaa, Naif enrolled in Islamic Studies, a common precursor to legal, educational, or religious professions in the region. He had an appetite for self-improvement, reading self-help books and listening daily to BBC radio. When he was twenty-three he married a woman named Yasmin, also from Al-Bayda, who chose him from among a string of suitors. Naif appealed to her, she told me, because he was “a man of principles.”

After graduating Naif moved to Saudi Arabia for work, teaching for several years and then becoming an entrepreneur. He opened two successful car repair shops but was eager for a new challenge. In 2011 protests erupted against Yemen’s autocratic president of thirty-three years, Ali Abdullah Saleh, who had long benefited from US support. God has given a gift to the people, Naif thought. The demonstrations swelled, mobilizing over 100,000 people in the streets of Sanaa. Saleh was ousted the following year, replaced by a transitional government run by Hadi, the former vice president. Naif returned home permanently the next year, eager to join in Yemen’s political transition.

Back in Al-Bayda, Naif was anointed as his clan’s sheikh. He began meeting with different tribes, encouraging older leaders to listen to the demands of the young organizers. At that time there was a guerrilla al-Qaeda presence in Al-Bayda. They held no territory, but Naif worried about their appeal for disenfranchised young people, and he focused on advocating for nonviolent methods of political change. Others took notice. In 2013 Hadi appointed Naif as an advisor for the governorate of Hajjah.

Naif considered it his job to implement the recommendations of a ten-month, inclusive “national dialogue” process that had brought together a variety of constituencies—from political parties, including the former ruling party and the Houthis, to youth movements—to draft a new constitution for Yemen. The final document outlined a federal system and, among other changes, reduced the power of tribes in governance. The transition, it specified, would occur without Yemen “losing its soul or self, so the great peoples adopt their awakening without abandoning their mettle, character, and values.”

But in September 2014 the fledgling democratic process crumbled when the Houthis, a Zaydi Shia movement officially known as Ansar Allah, staged a coup. (The Houthis had previously waged six wars against the government between 2004 and 2010.) The Yemeni security forces collapsed, and war ensued. Saudi Arabia, opposed to the Houthis due to their affiliation with Iran, mobilized an “Arab Coalition” of ten countries to defend Hadi’s government, initially including the UAE and Qatar. The coalition launched extensive air strikes on Houthi-held territory and imposed a naval blockade, and soon humanitarian advocates were accusing its members of war crimes. Human rights groups found that Saudi planes dropping US- and Britain-supplied bombs were disproportionately killing civilians and destroying medical clinics.

Meanwhile the UAE pursued its own strategy. To avoid a Yemeni government aligned with their adversary the Muslim Brotherhood, the Emiratis funded brutal proxy militias in the south, which detained and killed politicians, imams, and civilians with impunity. (They also employed American mercenaries.) The US continued to aid the Saudi-led campaign, setting up an intelligence cell in Riyadh, but was focused on eradicating the al-Qaeda network, sometimes aided by the Emirates, and launching its own semiregular drone strikes.

Amid these shifting alliances, Yemenis tried to survive a collapsing economy, famine, cholera, landmines, and cluster bombs. “Life collapsed in one fell swoop,” writes Bushra al-Maqtari in her introduction to What Have You Left Behind (2023), a collection of civilian testimonies. “The dark irony of it all is that the agitators are always either beneficiaries of the respective military powers on the inside, or reside in Arab or European capitals, far from the war raging in their own country.”

As the Houthis moved outward from Sanaa, Naif formed a coalition of local tribes to defend the province. The Al-Bayda Tribal Coalition (it later became the Al-Bayda Tribes Resistance) unified six clans with different political leanings—bringing together partisans of the General People’s Congress, the Islamic Islah Party, the Socialist Party, and the Nasserist Party, among others. Energetic and respected, Naif wore military fatigues to meetings. His public profile rose, and in December 2015 Hadi appointed Naif as governor. His first task was to convert the informal Tribal Coalition into a professional army unit of the Yemeni government: the new 117th Brigade, which had some 2,200 members and an army leader, received funding from the Saudis for operations. Naif participated in operational command meetings of the Arab Coalition. “My team and I were building a comprehensive plan to liberate, secure, and develop the province,” he explained. Then the UN listing arrived.

Within four months, Naif no longer felt he could govern. He knew Hadi’s government still needed the UN and international partners, and feared the terrorist accusations would taint Al-Bayda. He resigned. Without a purpose or direction, he spent hours pondering how he had ended up on the list. As governor he’d made a lot of enemies. Had he been framed for his religious beliefs, for having served as an imam in his youth? Or for his outspokenness about Saudi Arabia’s war crimes? Naif had criticized the Saudis in private meetings, arguing that they were illegally bombing civilian targets. He’d also clashed with the Emiratis, who he felt were diverting attention from fighting the Houthis to countering the Islah Party, considered a proxy of the Muslim Brotherhood. Meanwhile, the Houthis and the former Saleh regime were known to slander their enemies as AQAP. It was a mistake, Naif realized, not to have publicized his activities as governor more in the media, although some of his speeches against violent extremism are still visible on YouTube. “I’m not savvy,” he told me sheepishly.

In those days a memory came back to him, and he wondered if it had anything to do with the listing. One day at a military strategy meeting with representatives of the UAE, after he appeared on the US’s list but before the UN added him to theirs, an Emirati officer had pressured Naif for direct intelligence briefings. If he cooperated with them, he recalled the man saying, they could get the Americans to take his name off the list. Spying is illegal under Yemen’s constitution, and Naif told the officer he reported only to the Yemeni president. The Emiratis issued vague warnings about how the consequences would multiply, but Naif was too busy to take the threats seriously; he spent his time trekking between hospitals to visit the wounded, military bases to meet with army commanders, and government offices to request aid for the displaced and families of the dead. But now he wondered: Had the UAE fed the UN false intelligence to punish him for refusing to spy?

Naif needed a lawyer, but he had no idea who could represent him. One day he got a call from Shiban, the Arab Spring organizer, who was working with Reprieve, a British human rights organization specializing in counterterrorism cases. Shiban suggested Naif fly to Istanbul to meet with him and the head of Reprieve. Straightaway Naif booked a ticket, traveling via Khartoum, but when he arrived in Istanbul the Turkish authorities blocked his entry.

Dejected, he decided to stay in Sudan. Life in Al-Bayda had become increasingly dangerous. Earlier that year a US Special Forces raid to capture al-Qaeda militants had killed some twenty-five civilians, including nine children under the age of thirteen. Both the Houthis and al-Qaeda were targeting former and current members of Yemen’s government. Reprieve ultimately couldn’t take on Naif’s case and began searching for lawyers with expertise in sanctions.

Yasmin and the children joined Naif in Sudan, and in September 2017 he rented a farm outside Khartoum. In Al-Bayda, meanwhile, the Houthis swiftly advanced, gaining territory. Multiple factors likely contributed to the Houthi takeover, but al-Maisari told me that Naif’s absence had “crippled the province.”

After a difficult stretch in Sudan—the usually fierce Yasmin felt isolated and adrift in their new home—two fortuitous events occurred. The first was that Oman offered Naif and his family entry on account of his status as a tribal leader, overlooking the UN travel ban. The family moved to Muscat, then to Salalah, a small city on the Arabian Sea some two hours from the Yemeni border. The second was that Gavin Sullivan agreed to represent Naif before the UN.

Before he became Naif’s lawyer, Sullivan and his wife discussed the possibility that they too could end up on a blacklist. What if their finances were frozen? A retaliatory listing would have severe consequences. But Sullivan’s wife, who confronts powerful interests in her work as a labor union organizer, was in favor of taking on the case. Sullivan agreed to represent Naif on a pro bono basis before the UN. His legal team got to work; in June 2021, four years after Naif’s UN listing, they filed an appeal.

At the time the UN ombudsperson was Daniel Kipfer Fasciati, an experienced Swiss criminal judge. He reviewed the reasons for Naif’s listing: the Security Council alleged that Naif was associated with al-Qaeda, and had sanctioned him for

“participating in the financing, planning, facilitating, preparing, or perpetrating of acts or activities by, in conjunction with, under the name of, on behalf of, or in support of” and “supplying, selling or transferring arms and related materiel to” Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula.

The narrative summary—which was shared with Naif and Sullivan—furthermore stated that Naif was a senior official and a financial supporter of AQAP, obtained money for AQAP from parties outside Yemen, facilitated the expansion of AQAP in Al-Bayda, and transferred money and weapons to AQAP fighters. In addition, it alleged that Naif had “served as an AQAP facilitator who provided financial support to AQAP to help it take control of parts of Yemen…and financed AQAP training camps.” Naif vigorously denied all the allegations.

That summer Fasciati started comparing evidence shared by UN member states with Sullivan’s delisting petition. He learned that the US had requested Naif’s listing and that other states, including the Saudis, had submitted intelligence information. He met with these governments behind closed doors, then traveled to Oman to conduct interviews, including with al-Maisari and other high-ranking Yemeni officials. Naif slipped on a silvery gray suit and met with Fasciati in November 2021. Sullivan, without the money to pay for a flight, represented Naif via Zoom: over the years he and other lawyers had tried to get funders to support the Transnational Listing Project, but even progressive donors said they saw legal defense for listed people associated with al-Qaeda as a lost cause.

Fasciati walked Naif through the allegations, and then Sullivan and his team explained that many of Naif’s official activities as governor had seemingly been twisted into examples of terrorist activity. Naif had received external funding—but it was from Saudi Arabia for provincial military activities. He had organized not a terrorist base but an official army training camp for the 117th, which exists to this day. Naif’s pro bono legal team submitted forty pieces of evidence to Fasciati: army payment slips, photos of the camp, text messages from AQAP threatening to murder the man the UN now claimed belonged to them.

Particularly disturbing to Sullivan was that part of the listing seemed to stem from a fundamental misunderstanding by the US government of the relationship between Yemeni tribes and al-Qaeda. Tribal organization is particularly important in rural parts of Yemen, where the majority of the population lives. Western commentators and policy experts for years had falsely claimed that certain tribes were aiding al-Qaeda, when the reality was that individual recruitment to al-Qaeda was based not on tribal affiliation but on factors such as poverty and disenfranchisement. Some of the tribes in Al-Bayda with whom Naif had legitimate dealings, Sullivan came to think, had been conflated with AQAP, a problem documented by scholars such as Helen Lackner. “Particularly in the media, but also in officialdom, there has been a tendency to take a simplistic approach based on the widespread prejudices about tribes, and to link the concept of tribalism with the presence of al Qaeda and other jihadi groups,” Lackner writes.

Then there was the US’s history of muddled intelligence when it came to Yemen. The US has on multiple occasions admitted to acting on erroneous intel in the country, including in 2010, when they killed the deputy governor of Marib, one of former President Saleh’s political rivals, in a missile attack that relied on Yemeni government intelligence. A US official later said “we think we got played.” There are many other reports of US drone strikes hitting civilian targets in Yemen; a brief by the Atlantic Council stated in 2014 that “the United States frequently claims to have killed the same high-level figure multiple times, which raises serious questions about the accuracy of intelligence used to select targets as well as the precision of the strikes.” Tribal affiliation and false intelligence might have led to Naif’s initial listing by the US Treasury, but the UN listing, which other countries supported, seemed politically motivated. Still, Sullivan had no access to the original listing material, nor any way to question the US, Saudis, Emirates, or others.

After three years as ombudsperson, Fasciati resigned in June 2021, citing the office’s lack of independence. In public reports he criticized the institutional weakness of the position, explaining, for instance, that states periodically refused to grant him access to interview petitioners and that listing information could be of poor quality, sometimes gained under torture. But by the time he left in December most of his work on Naif’s case was complete.

In a publicly available report to the Security Council, Fasciati issued a scathing overview. The original listing rationale was seemingly in conflict with basic facts about the Yemeni war: “For example, a government military training camp was attributed to Al-Qaida, even though it could not possibly have been under the control of Al-Qaida.” Furthermore, “it could not be established whether the information had been collected by the intelligence services of different countries or had originated from one source and been shared by that source with the services of other countries,” raising the possibility that one state could have manipulated others.

In March 2022 the new ombudsperson, Richard Malanjum, shared the office’s official recommendation with Sullivan. The confidential report, which was delivered to the Security Council and which I reviewed, put its conclusion in stark terms: “Unlike any other case that I have considered so far, it is striking that the listing information and publicly available information about the Petitioner on the one hand, and the comments on it from the Petitioner and from other interviewed persons on the other hand, are diametrically opposed and irreconcilably contradictory.” The report states that intelligence from Saudi Arabia was blatantly wrong, citing claims that Naif was in Yemen supporting terrorist activity when he had already left the country. (Information about any intelligence from other UN member states supporting the allegations is redacted.) The ombudsperson’s office found the total accusations so implausible, given Naif’s public persona as a statesman, that they only made sense if Naif was a double agent. The ombudsperson found no proof this was the case, and while he could not state with certainty why Naif had been listed, a “likely hypothesis is that at least some of the false accusations were intentional.”

Naif was at home eating dinner when Shiban called from London. “Do you remember the promise you made to take Yasmin and the family on vacation to Turkey?” Shiban asked. “Yes, and I’m sticking to my promise,” Naif replied, wondering what Shiban was on about. “You should start packing,” Shiban said, his normally steady voice trembling. “You’ve been delisted.” It was a moment, Naif told me, of “indescribable joy.” News travels fast around the Yemeni community in Salalah; guests began arriving at Naif’s house to celebrate. They lingered long into the night.

3.

When Sullivan, Shiban, and I arrived at Naif’s roomy house in Salalah on a humid weekday in October 2022, Naif jumped out of the gate grinning. “Welcome! Welcome, Gavin,” he said, kissing the man on both cheeks. “You did a brilliant job with my case.” It was Naif’s first time meeting his lawyer in person. Naif, who has thick eyebrows and a broad nose, was sprightly in a white robe and brown leather slip-on sandals. He ushered us in past two parrots and up to the roof, where a circle of cushioned chairs made an informal salon next to a gurgling fountain.

The sun fell slowly, illuminating the astroturf. Naif sat cross-legged on a chair, snacking on dates as Yemenis arrived to pay their respects to Sullivan: the former head of the teacher’s union of Al-Bayda, the former governor of the island of Socotra, various sheikhs, the head of the Marib Emergency Unit, the former minister of fish. The guests discussed the events that had brought them to Salalah: one had been shot protesting for democracy in Al-Bayda, another detained by a UAE-run proxy militia for nine months.

“Our neighbors, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, don’t share the same hopes we do—we want pluralism,” the former representative of Al-Bayda’s teacher’s union remarked. “Welcome to the Yemeni sessions,” joked Shiban, who, dressed in a faded t-shirt and jeans, still looked very much the student organizer. The men teased Shiban, who had made the local TV news for banning khat at his wedding. He was against it, primarily, for climate reasons, as the crop requires an immense amount of water—an unpopular stance among the guests who liked to occasionally imbibe.

Amid the chatter, Naif leaned over and informed Sullivan that he had recently flown to Istanbul to visit some friends. Upon arrival, he was denied entry, detained for twelve hours in a holding cell, and sent back to Muscat. Sullivan pulled out an electronic tablet and began taking notes. The airport officials had given Naif a piece of paper in Turkish, which he now handed over. “The hardest part,” Sullivan whispered, not wanting to distract from the revelry, “is that when you come off the UN list, you stay on other lists.”

This had happened to Sullivan’s other clients, too. One man I spoke with, Youssef Abdaoui, a Tunisian living in Italy, had been taken off the UN list in 2014. When he flew to Romania to reunite with his wife and children, he was arrested at the airport and deported. The authorities, Sullivan said, had given him a twenty-one-year travel ban due to “an unspecified threat to public order.” Sullivan has been unable to determine why Romania denied Abdaoui entry. No process exists to compensate delisted individuals for the years they were blacklisted, erase the character assassination that lives indefinitely on the Internet, or remove them from national lists.

The next morning I found Sullivan hunched over his laptop in a coffee shop, looking for a lawyer in Istanbul who could challenge Naif’s Turkish entry ban. There were only three days left to appeal the decision in a local court. That night, as we walked through downtown Salalah, inhaling the fumes of diesel exhaust and passing shops selling jugs of amber Yemeni honey, thought to cure all manner of ailments, a white sedan pulled up. “You’re Naif’s friends!” the driver said, grinning. “I’ll take you to eat Yemeni food!” Sullivan peered at the man warily over his glasses. “Who are you?” he asked, scanning the vehicle and the street. On a recent trip to Tunisia to conduct interviews with listed individuals, Sullivan found that his hotel room had been broken into; state intelligence officials trailed him on motorbikes. But it turned out Naif had sent the man to make sure we did not eat at a mediocre restaurant.

Representing listed individuals had consumed Sullivan. In addition to his case work, he was researching the UN’s use of global technologies for predictive watchlisting. At the end of 2017 the Security Council passed resolution 2396, which directed the ISIL and Al-Qaeda Sanctions Committee to expand the 1267 List to target “foreign terrorist fighters,” a vague term used primarily to describe Americans and Europeans who join armed groups abroad. It mandated that all countries create watchlists of “known and suspected terrorists” and share them internationally. The first Trump administration had pushed for the resolution (then-counterterrorism coordinator Nathan Sales boasted at a conference that “by making watchlists mandatory, the Security Council has taken a U.S. initiative and made it the international norm”), but it also received support from private corporations and other powerful countries. “It’s a great example of US, Russia, and Chinese interests aligning,” Eric Rosand, a senior State Department official under the Obama administration, told me.

The UN’s Office of Counter-Terrorism now owns and installs tracking software called goTravel, created by the Dutch government, that scoops up airline passenger details in countries that install it, analyzing names and itineraries for “suspicious patterns” to inform decisions about who is allowed to board a plane or cross a border. In 2021 the office’s deputy, a former US State Department official named Raffi Gregorian, told West Point’s The Countering Terrorism Center Sentinel that to better predict terrorist travel they were working on “algorithms that tell the data systems what to look for, like people between age twenty and twenty-five traveling from Mogadishu to Nairobi and then on to Frankfurt, if that happens to be a travel pattern of interest.” (I emailed Gregorian several times, but he did not reply.) A UN pilot project called goFintel has experimented with developing algorithms to identify “suspicious” individuals and ban them from making financial transactions, including based on open-source social media data and the 1267 List.

When Naif first came to Oman he didn’t have a residence permit. Once, as he was driving about town running errands, he was stopped by the police and had to wait on the side of the road until they verified his identity and status. It was unnerving, so he stopped going out. The Omanis initially told him that they didn’t want to upset the Americans or the UN by making his stay officially legal. But prominent Yemenis advocated on his behalf, and about a year later the Omanis issued the permit.

Now when Naif needs space, he hops in the car and heads for the canyons and wadis that rise behind Salalah’s coastal plain. He hikes a trail through a nature reserve that meanders past waterfalls and between boulders, descending to a bright turquoise river. During the monsoon season the ground turns a feverish green, but the rest of the year it’s dry and cracked from the heat. Solitude in Salalah is rare, but out here it is possible to think.

Often, as Naif walks, he worries about his debts. Initially he had received income from his car repair businesses in Saudi Arabia, but eventually he was forced to sell those businesses and other investments for cash. Today he is still blocked from receiving any money through banks because of the US Treasury sanctions and has fallen deep in arears. Still he was grateful, because his family’s wealth and political connections had kept him afloat. He knew that other men on the list had experienced far worse.

Naif’s marriage with Yasmin had been strained by the relocations: two years ago she considered a divorce. Lately they were doing better. (Naif married a second wife a few years ago, as is customary in some parts of Yemen, but she was more shielded from the listing’s fallout, since the family had already settled in Oman.) Naif and Yasmin frequently discussed how to protect their family. They did not want their children to be surveilled, and they forbade their older sons from visiting Yemen, terrified that they could be somehow targeted, kidnapped, or killed.

Sullivan, who is now at the University of Edinburgh, is filing an appeal for Naif with the American government to get him removed from the Treasury’s list. This is likely to be extraordinarily difficult: according to a 2020 analysis done by West Point’s Combatting Terrorism Center, between 2001 and 2016 the Treasury listed some 718 people as Specially Designated Global Terrorists; only twenty-five have been delisted while they were still alive. The Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which manages the process, does not have to share the basis of their allegations or name major witnesses during an appeal. Listed individuals can only submit a petition once. During his research into another client listed by both the US and the UN, Kamel Darraji, Sullivan stumbled via Wikileaks upon cables the State Department had sent in 2009 indicating that they found no grounds for Darraji’s listing. Today, although he was delisted by the UN in 2012, Darraji is still a Treasury sanctioned terrorist. He has been on the list for twenty-two years. (OFAC did not respond to a request for comment.)

Outside of the Treasury’s terrorist sanctions lists, which as of this April contained some 17,000 names, the US is increasingly using sanctions to target journalists and political opponents. In a strange twist, last year the Trump administration sanctioned a former 1267 List ombudsperson—the Canadian lawyer and judge Kimberly Prost—for her more recent work as a judge of the International Criminal Court, along with eight of her colleagues. The US has also sanctioned multiple Palestinian human rights organizations, as well as the UN investigator Francesca Albanese, who successfully sued the US government. Prost, in an interview with Al Jazeera, reflected on the effects of the listing. “I thought I had a good understanding of the impact of sanctions. But until you experience it, it doesn’t become real to you,” she said. “Immediately, you have no credit cards. It doesn’t matter where they were issued or what bank, because of the control of the Americans over the SWIFT system. It cripples you in our modern world.”

Naif’s inclusion on the Treasury’s list has not prevented members of the American government from approaching him for intelligence. Naif met them first in Salalah at the Millennium Hotel, a family-friendly resort with a generous breakfast buffet. Later they met in Muscat in the Officers Club of the Omani Royal Court. A man who called himself Mike and who Naif described as “looking like Sullivan”—middle-aged, white, short dark hair flecked with gray—wanted to get Naif’s views on countering al-Qaeda in Al-Bayda. “Not by drones,” Naif recalls telling him. “We need to work along two tracks: for those who don’t have jobs, we create opportunities, and for those who are involved in criminal acts, they go through a fair judicial process.” He connected Mike to security officials in Al-Bayda, helping him out as a favor to the Omanis. The Americans promised to work on delisting him, but the years passed without any change.

When I spoke to Naif recently, the Americans in Muscat were still soliciting his insights into Yemen’s grinding war. The country remains divided between the Houthi-controlled north and west, including Sanaa, and the south, where the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), Yemen’s internationally recognized government, is based in the coastal port of Aden. Saudi Arabia and the US continue to back the PLC. The UAE-funded Southern Transitional Council split from the PLC last year and tried to capture two southern provinces, but the PLC regained the territory in late 2025, and the UAE withdrew from the country earlier this year.

Meanwhile, in response to the Israeli genocide in Gaza, the Houthis have attacked ships in the Red Sea and fired missiles at targets in Israel. Both the Biden and Trump administrations launched retaliatory attacks against the Houthis, until the Omanis brokered an official cease-fire. The Red Sea, the anthropologist Samar Al-Bulushi told me, has become the most militarized space in the world. In all this the interests of regular Yemenis have been ignored. “Around me the list of the dead grows longer and longer: family, relatives, friends, neighbors—all civilians killed for no reason,” al-Maqtari wrote in What Have You Left Behind? That list is now over 350,000 names long.

One afternoon while we were in Salalah, Naif piled his younger children in the car—Saba, Sultan, Aya, and Salah—along with Sullivan, Shiban, and myself and headed to the beach. We stopped to buy the kids ice cream bars, and then pulled up at the Arabian Prosthetics Center, where specialists rehabilitated dozens of war-wounded Yemenis (it has since shut down). Close to 90 percent of the patients had stepped on landmines. Naif helped people in Al-Bayda travel to the facility, then visited them while they were fitted for new limbs. Inside it smelled of fresh plaster and paint, and the ovens were firing to mold the prosthetics.

On the drive out of town we passed long lines for drive-through coffee and half-built homes wedged against gentle umber hills. Naif stared ahead as he drove, unusually silent. After passing a military checkpoint on the town’s outskirts, we turned down a narrow road that curved up and around a bend; beyond was a gleam of blue. The children shrieked and stuck their hands out the open windows. Naif took them on a walk, up a rock-hewn path along a cliff edging the sea. Tucked into his belt was a Jambiya that used to belong to his father. We passed a few tourists as three-year-old Sultan raced ahead of us barefoot, impervious to danger. Saba and Aya clamored up a ledge and called for their dad. Naif hurried over, extending his arms wide. The girls jumped.

Life here was safe, and Naif was indebted to the Omanis. But he dreamed that his children would have a more expansive future. Aya likes to read and loves art. Saba is interested in medicine; Naif thinks she might be a doctor, Sultan a military commander, Salah a pilot. They know they’re Yemeni, and Naif tells them stories of the smoky green mountains in Al-Bayda, but he doesn’t want them to live in the past. He worries the listing will somehow affect them when they least expect it, when they try to board a plane or open a bank account. His oldest child is about to graduate from high school and wants to study cybersecurity abroad, but because of the sanctions Naif cannot transfer funds for tuition.

The place Naif most wants to go is Yemen, where he yearns to be part of the political process again. “In Yemen’s political scene, if you’re not present, you’re basically gone,” Naif said. Despite the UN delisting, high-ranking Yemeni officials have signaled that in the country’s current political climate it’s still improbable that he will be able to return, as long as he remains listed by the American government. Sometimes Naif thinks about the strangers who made that initial decision. It was a simple series of administrative functions: an entry on a spreadsheet, a line on a No Fly list. This data did not represent a life, but it could permanently alter one. Naif still holds out hope that the US will clear his name. Until then, if there’s one thing the past ten years have taught him, it’s how to wait.

entries.title: All of Life
entries.summary: In the Review’s June 25 issue, Joe Dunthorne writes about a recent oral history of the New York School poets and poses himself a challenge: “How to analyze a poetics of irreverence and improvisation—of life experienced in a perpetual present—without stifling precisely these qualities?” His essay suggests that the poetry in the scene, by writers […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
This article is part of a regular series of conversations with the Review’s contributors; read past entries here and sign up for our email newsletter to get them delivered to your inbox each week.

In the Review’s June 25 issue, Joe Dunthorne writes about a recent oral history of the New York School poets and poses himself a challenge: “How to analyze a poetics of irreverence and improvisation—of life experienced in a perpetual present—without stifling precisely these qualities?” His essay suggests that the poetry in the scene, by writers ranging from Frank O’Hara and John Ashbery to Alice Notley and Eileen Myles, emerged in part from their social and family lives. The vivacity of their work drew from the eclecticism of their world, or, as Dunthorne quotes Notley, “We’re inside each other’s lives.” “Despite the disputes and grievances that run through these pages,” he continues, “there is a sense that what survives of these poets, apart from their poetry, is the generative and spiky sociability that brought them together in the first place.”

Dunthorne is an eclectic writer in his own right. He is the author of three novels, including his debut, Submarine (2008), which was adapted into a film by Richard Ayoade; a collection of poetry, O Positive (2019); and a family memoir, Children of Radium (2025), which was reviewed in our pages by Francine Prose. His criticism, essays, poems, and stories have appeared in, among many other places, The Paris Review, The Guardian, The Atlantic, and the London Review of Books.

I wrote to Dunthorne this month to ask him about the sociability of art, writing while broke, and the first New York School poet: William Wordsworth.

Aleander Santos: What was your first encounter with the New York School poets? What did you think of them, then and now? Do you think a scene like the School could exist today?

Joe Dunthorne: I was lucky enough to be taught by Daniel Kane at the University of East Anglia when I was an undergraduate. At that time, he’d just published All Poets Welcome: The Lower East Side Poetry Scene in the 1960s,and he introduced us not just to the poetry but to the whole social world of it. They were instantly alluring, this witty, catty, playful coterie who seemed to toss out brilliant poems while talking on the phone or riding the Staten Island Ferry. They made it look not just easy but fun. I loved the irreverence and the silliness of their work, and it opened up possibilities in my own writing. In particular, I remember reading Frank O’Hara’s anti-poetic manifesto, Personism, and thinking: these are my people. I still feel the same today. For me, the New York School is a bottomless source of permission. It’s an open invitation. What I appreciate even more as I get older is the importance of their sociability, how they rubbed up against each other, sparked off each other, argued, had affairs, borrowed money, raised children, but ultimately were all deeply committed to one another. That feels profound. And all the while the poems were just falling off them.

As for the question of whether that kind of scene could exist today, I have to hope that it could! Just not in New York or London. I’d like to think that somewhere a city has the right blend of affordability, sociability, and opportunity to create the conditions for what Lewis Warsh called the “24-hour-a-day salon.”

Many of the writers of the first generation were well off, with Harvard educations and prestigious careers. But people in the second generation often came from harder backgrounds. How do you think these different situations influenced their poetry? Is it possible to make sincere art while also thinking about making money?

One answer to that question is to quote “Motto of the Whores and Poets Guild,” the very short poem that the second-generation poets Alice Notley and Ted Berrigan wrote together: “You’ll do good if you play it like you’re not getting paid./But you’ll do it better if the motherfuckers pay you.” One reading of that poem is, yes, great poetry will emerge, regardless of how much money is available, but having money buys the poets the time to do their best work. I think that’s true. But I also think that money and the lack of it can be a productive subject in its own right. Ted Berrigan has a wonderful riff in Train Ride:

I like Credit Cards



Alas, I can’t pay the bills,

but I always spend with the Credit Card

in a terrific way!!

*

I take people to terrific



Restaurants!

*

I go to England!

*

I buy somebody their



return ticket, because they’re

broke.

*

I buy a couple of terrific



shirts,

& a pair of pants

*

I like to give people



money

*

I hate to be given money. It’s embarrassing!

I do like



to get money in the mail.

& I like to get paid lots of money



for doing something like reading, talking, or

publishing

*

How come I can’t get paid



just for writing?

*

I do like to get presents



spontaneously given,

or just for me.

*

But it’s socially awkward that



some people for almost no reason

have money, & some don’t.

On the question about the right conditions in which to make “sincere art,” part of what I love about the New York School is that they would never worry about that! It reminds me of a line from Personism where O’Hara talks about the moment his lofty ideas get so lofty that he can’t think about them anymore, “and that’s when refreshment arrives.” For me, the New York School is all about instinct and receptiveness. It encourages a freedom to bring all of life into the poetry, whether you’re swanning around Manhattan with your fancy art friends or you’ve never been to New York. It can all go in.

Advertisement

You write both poetry and fiction. For these genres, what’s your writing process like? How do you start?

Writing poetry is pretty constant for me. It sometimes feels like a semiconscious biological process. Like burping. I’ve never written a diary, but I at least have my poems, which act as a record of my life. I love that I can write them anywhere. On a bus or train or while waiting for a doctor’s appointment or on my phone at night, lit up beneath the duvet. I write my absolute worst work when I sit down and think: now it’s time to write a poem about this important life event! Conversely, my best work usually emerges from a complete lack of expectation. All of which feels quite New York School.

Fiction, however, is another thing entirely. I cannot stumble my way into writing a novel. It has to be somewhat regimented and bureaucratic. I often make a graph to track my daily progress. It’s not romantic. I do still try and bring freedom and playfulness into my process but, in the end, I know that I will have to just put in the hours, the years, of redrafting and restructuring. One of the hardest things is that, for me, novels do not get easier with practice. The more I know about writing one, the harder it is to proceed.

This New York School essay was fairly research heavy. How does writing nonfiction that requires research differ from writing fiction or poetry? Do you feel like you edit or revise differently in each mode?

To me, nonfiction feels more curatorial. It’s about collecting and sifting through information and then putting the right pieces in the right order. With this piece in particular I was inspired by a recent nonfiction book by Rachel Cockerell called Melting Point. It’s a history of a Jewish Zionist project in Texas that’s told entirely through quotations from primary sources. Cockerell absents herself from the narrative—although of course she is there as a curator, an arranger. With this New York School poets essay, I didn’t go quite as far as she does, but I wanted to include as much quotation as I could, to try and make the piece feel a bit like a house party at which you overhear all these different and often contradictory opinions. It helps that the interviews in the book that occasioned the review, Conversations with New York School Poets, are so fun. New York School poets don’t know how to be boring!

What are some works by the New York School poets that you think are most worth reading? Teaching?

There are so many! Here are a few favorites, a mix of New York School founders and contemporary poets who are New York School–inflected.

Shorter ones:

  • “[Sonnet] You jerk you didn’t call me up,” by Bernadette Mayer
  • “The Problem of Anxiety,” by John Ashbery
  • “For the Record I Really Wish I Talked Less but I Literally Cannot Help It,” by Sasha Debevec-McKenney

Longer ones:

  • “The Circus,” by Kenneth Koch
  • Train Ride, by Ted Berrigan
  • “The Ex-Girlfriends Are Back from the Wilderness,” by Hera Lindsay Bird

Finally, here’s a New York School poem written in London in 1808. I see this as Wordsworth preemptively channeling Frank O’Hara. My hot take: Wordsworth was wasted on the countryside:

  • “St. Paul’s,” by William Wordsworth

What are you reading now?

In poetry, I just read and loved Dean Browne’s poetry collection After Party, which finds a really happy balance between New York School chattiness and a more structured Irish tradition. Try this one.

In fiction, I just finished Hunchback by Saou Ichikawa (translated by Polly Barton), which felt like an electric shock of a book. It’s very alive and sexy and strange. I recommend.

After that, I wanted to read something a bit different, so I went with Neuromancer by William Gibson, which is just a joy. The dystopian cyberpunk future, as imagined in 1984, is as awe-inspiring as ever. (In many ways, it is a much preferable dystopia to the one we are currently living in.) Gibson is also just a brilliant stylist.

entries.title: La Querelle des Femmes
entries.summary: In 2015, I was on a panel at New York’s Museum of Arts and Design titled “Do We Need Exhibitions Just for Women?” As I remember, most of the participants agreed that we did, though some expressed concerns about ghettoization or weariness at having a conversation they’d had many times before. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In 2015, I was on a panel at New York’s Museum of Arts and Design titled “Do We Need Exhibitions Just for Women?” As I remember, most of the participants agreed that we did, though some expressed concerns about ghettoization or weariness at having a conversation they’d had many times before. As the youngest participant, I understood their frustration, but I had no doubt that the answer was an emphatic yes. It seemed obvious that as long as we had gender inequality, we also needed correctives.

Asking myself the same question today, I’m still inclined to answer in the affirmative, but with markedly less gusto. Over the last decade I’ve witnessed the ways that progress can seem linear only to suddenly loop back on itself. Women face increased misogyny and discrimination in many places, including the US. Even in the art world, the situation is retrograde: a 2022 report by the journalists Charlotte Burns and Julia Halperin found that only 11 percent of acquisitions and 14.9 percent of exhibitions at thirty-one American museums were devoted to women, despite them accounting for almost half of the country’s working artists.

The catalog of “The Woman Question, 1550–2025,” a recent exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw, traces the origins of all-women exhibitions to the late nineteenth century, the early years of the first-wave feminist movement. Female artists started societies like the Palette Club and the Union des femmes peintres et sculpteurs in cities like Chicago and Paris, showing and promoting the work of their members at a time when women in the arts faced a range of professional exclusions, including being barred from life-drawing classes and most art academies.

Such shows flourished until the beginning of the twentieth century, when they suddenly dwindled, and the men curating and writing art surveys and textbooks began editing women out of history. As the curator of “The Woman Question,” Alison M. Gingeras, notes in the catalog, “Ironically, it would seem that the rise of suffragist and first-wave feminist movements that won women the right to vote produced a misogynous backlash in the field of art.” It took almost an entire century for the all-women exhibition to return amid the heyday of second-wave feminism in the 1970s—and when it did, it became a vehicle for reclaiming forgotten histories.

One of the most important such shows of the time was “Women Artists: 1550–1950,” organized in 1977 by the art historians Ann Sutherland Harris and Linda Nochlin at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (before traveling to museums in three other cities). Harris and Nochlin attempted to rewrite the patriarchal canon, gathering works by eighty-three artists from twelve countries in what the press release described as “the first international exhibition of works by women artists.” They concentrated on historical painting but found wide range within that category, moving from the Italian Renaissance artist Sofonisba Anguissola to the French realist Rosa Bonheur to the Russian modernist Natalia Goncharova to the American Abstract Expressionist Lee Krasner, and featuring many artists who were largely unknown to audiences at the time. Still, the vast majority of the figures they included were white and Western, and Harris and Nochlin acknowledged and defended this narrow purview in their catalog. The omissions, they wrote, meant “not so much that the present exhibition is limited but rather that the possibilities for future ones exploring the work of women in the arts are unlimited: we look forward to future developments.”

“The Woman Question, 1550–2025” took up this challenge by bringing the story of women’s art into the present and greatly diversifying the ranks of its practitioners. Like her predecessors, Gingeras eschewed any attempt to be comprehensive, instead homing in on a series of motifs that have appeared in art by women across nearly five centuries, including self-representation, surrealism, motherhood, sexuality, and war. The sweeping show was anchored by the works of well-known artists—including Artemisia Gentileschi, Leonor Fini, Louise Bourgeois, Tracey Emin, and Catherine Opie—but prioritized the delight of discovery. There were surprising selections by names I knew well and many more names that were unfamiliar to me, such as the modernists Charley Toorop (Dutch) and Fahrelnissa Zeid (Turkish). Gingeras paid particular attention to Poland and Eastern Europe—including, for example, work by the contemporary Polish artists Katarzyna Górna and Zuzanna Hertzberg—and carefully placed formally educated artists in conversation with those who were self-taught. A section titled “Anonymous Was a Woman” included a painting and accompanying text relating the art historian Beata Purc’s case for why a Renaissance artist known only as the Brunswick Monogrammist may have been Mayken Verhulst, Pieter Brueghel the Elder’s mother-in-law.

Gingeras writes in the catalog that “inventories alone do not change patriarchal power structures; continual deep scholarship does.” This idea has a long history, though by now it might sound a bit more like a hopeful mantra than like an assertion of fact. “The Woman Question” was named for a literary genre of sorts that flourished in early modern Europe; thinkers both male and female—perhaps the most famous of whom was Christine de Pizan—wrote about la querelle des femmes, debating the status and nature of women. Were they all temptresses? Inferior to men? Or were they capable of reason and worthy of education? Centuries have gone by since then. Art has been made. Books have been written. Laws have been passed and repealed and then passed again. Freedoms have been hard won. Yet people keep finding new ways to ask the woman question. And so, no matter how weary we may be, we keep answering.

Advertisement

In what I can only describe as a punk move, “The Woman Question” opened with a gallery devoted to beheading. It was part of a larger first section titled “Femmes Fortes,” which took its name from a genre of paintings that flourished in seventeenth-century Europe, depicting biblical and historical heroines. Among the favorite subjects of the period were the princess Salomé, who requested and received the head of John the Baptist, and the widow Judith, who beheaded the Assyrian general Holofernes. (In lieu of a decapitation, one work on display depicted the biblical story of the Israelite Yael, who nailed a peg into the skull of the Canaanite general Sisera.) One of the most famous examples of the genre, Gentileschi’s visceral rendering of Judith in the act from around 1620, was not part of the show, but Gingeras did include her empathetic painting of an anguished and naked Susanna, from the Old Testament, being harassed by two elderly men.

Instead of historical works, though, the show’s small initial gallery held five modern and contemporary interpretations of the classic stories. Among them was a striking self-portrait from around 1929 by the Chicago-based artist Macena Barton, who depicts herself as an unapologetically nude, almost magician-like Salomé, clutching a scythe in one hand and a red curtain in the other; the fabric trails on the floor, where John the Baptist’s head rests on an ornate tray. Barton’s stance presages Cindy Sherman’s in a photograph that hung nearby, Untitled #228 (1990), which stars Sherman as Judith, dressed in a red gown and grasping a wrinkled dummy head of Holofernes. The works in the gallery conveyed a provocative range of emotional states, from the calm surreality of Barton’s Salomé to the sublimated rage of Betty Tompkins’s Women Words (Artemisia Gentileschi #2) (2024), which features sexist epithets overlaid on a copy of one of the Renaissance artist’s compositions. The cumulative effect was one of radical power: women dominating men, a tale as old as time.

The show also dealt inventively with other, more quotidian subject matter. In a section on motherhood, explicit images of birth and abortion—and images of queer and exhausted mothers—complicated idyllic mainstream conventions. One of the most surprising works was a contemporary replica, by the Franco-Brazilian artist Rebecca Campeau, of the “machine,” a medical doll used by the eighteenth-century French midwife Angélique Marguerite Le Boursier du Coudray to teach fellow midwives and simulate births. It’s a life-size, anatomically accurate linen and leather model of a woman’s pelvis, birth canal, and baby—an object born of need that reflects astonishing ingenuity and agency.

Meanwhile, a section titled “Wartime Women” focused on intimate or mundane scenes of violence rather than militaristic tributes or grand battles. Two small paintings by the Roma artist Ceija Stojka, one of several Holocaust survivors included (and also the subject of a recent exhibition at New York’s Drawing Center), portrayed Nazi soldiers humiliating prisoners while frenzied flocks of birds fill the sky. Works by contemporary Ukrainian artists were mostly more oblique, referencing the ongoing war through expressive, gestural paintings of solitary or abstracted figures; one by Lesia Khomenko shows a woman whose body has been reduced to a ghostly collection of brushstrokes by the force of an explosion.

But the show gave the most space to self-portraits, which filled two linked sections, one focused tightly on images depicting artists at work and the other including all manner of self-portraits. The quality and scope of work on view here was stunning. Gingeras brought together pieces by old masters like Anguissola (Italian, c.1532–1625) and Angelica Kauffman (Swiss, 1741–1807) with those of contemporary practitioners like Lisa Brice (South African, b. 1968) and Somaya Critchlow (British, b. 1993).

Given such a mix, the galleries could easily have become a hodgepodge, but Gingeras organized them into revealing juxtapositions and insightful thematic groupings, highlighting how different practitioners have riffed on consistent tropes, like the front-facing gaze and the inclusion of the artist’s accoutrements. Marie-Nicole Vestier-Dumont holds a palette in one hand and the cloth on her infant’s crib in another, as if to balance the two; Toorop places her palette behind her head so that it becomes a halo. A patchwork quilt by the self-taught African American artist Yvonne Wells, which shows her speaking into a megaphone in front of a US flag, hung near paintings by several self-taught Polish artists, creating an exchange about autodidacticism. A full-length, nude sculpture by the trans artist Puppies Puppies—a bronze cast of her body, including her breasts and penis, on a pedestal bearing the word “WOMAN”—stood at the end of a row of bodily sculptures, both illuminating the tradition she is working in and against and proposing her figure as a kind of culmination of an evolution of womanhood.

Advertisement

The feminist art historian Griselda Pollock writes in the catalog of “The Woman Question” that throughout the history of the all-women show, curators have felt compelled to “challenge the typical format of the narrative of Art History—charting art across eras, periods, styles, and movements crowned by a male genius.” Every exhibition, in other words, is a rejoinder as well as an expression of an independent vision. What made the show in Warsaw thrilling was that it felt like the women were talking first and foremost to each other, forming a chorus of female voices from across time and place, all shaping and insisting on their own selfhood.

Still, “The Woman Question” was not immune to the mandate that shaped its predecessors. On my last day in Warsaw I visited the nineteenth-century art galleries at the city’s National Museum. There, on one wall of a small room, a curator had organized a row of self-portraits by artists working on the cusp of the new century. The subjects exuded confidence as they stared at the viewer from their colorful canvases. They were all men. Gingeras’s carefully composed ensemble seemed to me like a direct rebuttal.

If self-representation was the greatest strength of “The Woman Question,” it was also the show’s most apparent weakness. The exhibition consisted almost entirely of figurative painting and sculpture. There was a logic to this: as Gingeras writes in the catalog, it “make[s] this continuity of women’s authorship legible over such a long span of art history.” (And, as she told me when we spoke, it made the show more accessible.) But it also limited the story that “The Woman Question” could tell. Centuries of female creativity have produced far more than representational art in traditional media.

The show’s omissions were highlighted in part by the other work on view in the museum. The same floor featured four small feminist exhibitions collectively titled “The City of Women”; the art historian Julia Bryan-Wilson’s contribution, which focused on allusive abstraction, was a standout. Upstairs, there were solo shows devoted to two very different abstract artists: the Polish modernist Maria Jarema and the Ethiopian American painter Julie Mehretu. These exhibitions usefully expanded on “The Woman Question,” but they also pointed to other pathways it could have taken.

I can picture a version of the show that incorporated more diverse work into Gingeras’s thematic structure. How might the conversation between the self-portraits have deepened if, amid a sea of paintings, there appeared Adrian Piper’s What Will Become of Me (1985–ongoing), a collection of jars holding her cut hair and fingernails? How would the gallery on motherhood have felt different if Louise Bourgeois had been represented not by figurative prints but by one of her more abstract fabric sculptures? The show already contained several such moments. The early gallery that housed Gentileschi’s Susanna, for instance, also included a video of Yoko Ono’s harrowing Cut Piece (1964), a performance in which she invited the audience to cut off pieces of her clothing. The connection was surprising and generative, suggesting continuity across centuries and continents between the ways women have made sense of violence against them.  

“The Woman Question” did not aspire to be comprehensive, but it did seek to reflect how women have imagined and asserted themselves through their art. What about the women who engineered new styles and techniques because the ones available couldn’t hold what they wanted to say? Hilma af Klint pioneered abstraction as an outlet for her spiritualism; Helen Frankenthaler soaked her canvases with paint she had thinned to make the color flatter and more ethereal; Senga Nengudi twisted pantyhose into bulging shapes that evoke women’s bodies. (Nengudi’s work appeared in Bryan-Wilson’s “City of Women” exhibition.) By largely omitting more formal work, as well as a wider scope of media, “The Woman Question” not only neglected this history, but also inadvertently confined its subjects to a narrowed range of experience.

Though “The Woman Question” did not include much expressly political art, most visitors surely arrived with an awareness of the history unfolding just outside the museum. In 1989 the Polish people freed themselves from Soviet rule and reinstated democracy, thanks largely to Solidarity, an opposition movement that grew out of a trade union. But when the leaders of Solidarity established their new government, they sold out Polish women: bowing to pressure from the Catholic Church, they passed an ordinance that made it more difficult to obtain a legal abortion. This was a sharp reversal from prior decades, when pregnant people had been able to get abortions with relative ease—so much so that women from Sweden were known to travel to Poland to access the procedure.

Restrictions have continued to accrue. In 2016 parliament debated a total abortion ban, catalyzing a movement called Polish Women’s Strike, which held enormous demonstrations filled with black-clad protesters mourning the proposed death of their rights. That ban failed, but abortion was largely outlawed in 2020, when Poland’s constitutional court ruled that abortions in cases of fetal anomaly were prohibited. The judgment set off another round of protests, co-organized by the Polish Women’s Strike, in which hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets despite restrictions on gathering imposed due to Covid-19; the demonstrations were the largest in the country since the fall of communism.

Photographs from some of these events could be seen in the hallway outside “The Woman Question,” as part of the artist Karolina Gembara’s “City of Women” show about reproductive rights. Shot by members of Poland’s grassroots Archive of Public Protests, they captured flashes of people in the streets, holding up coat hangers and middle fingers against dark, imperceptible backgrounds. The images were reproduced as takeaway posters and placed in stacks on wedge pedestals on the ground. Standing over them, I had an acute sense of the tension between the almost utopian world that was represented inside the museum and the hostile one outside its walls. One of the values of art is to help us envision how things could be different. It offers a space for imagining other realities, if not a way out of the one in which we live. “The Woman Question” did so by offering a rich vision of female creativity and solidarity. Perhaps most striking, it refused to make the case for women’s place in art history, instead simply asserting it as fact. This suggests a potential model. The Polish lawmakers banning abortion are, in their own way, asking the woman question. What would happen if we stopped answering and instead rejected its terms?

entries.summary: In 1954, with the ending of French colonial rule in Southeast Asia, the Geneva Accords established Laos as an independent state, led by the Royal Lao government. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In 1954, with the ending of French colonial rule in Southeast Asia, the Geneva Accords established Laos as an independent state, led by the Royal Lao government. Five years later, however, the Pathet Lao, backed by the communist government of North Vietnam, initiated a civil war that escalated, along with the Vietnam War, until 1975. Although the United States, which supported the Royal Lao government, signed an agreement with the Soviet Union and North Vietnam in 1962 guaranteeing that Laos would be neutral territory during the Vietnam War, Soviet-backed troops began ferrying supplies to the Viet Cong through Laos in 1964.

In response, the United States dropped two million tons of bombs on the country to try to disrupt that supply line. Nearly a third of the 270 million small cluster bombs dropped on Laos never exploded, and by some estimates, at least 20,000 people have been killed by unexploded ordnance since the war ended. Roughly 400,000 Hmong people lived in Laos at the start of the war (out of a population of more than 2 million), primarily farmers who lived in the country’s highland and mountain regions, maintaining a distinct culture and language. The Hmong community largely supported the Royal Lao government, and the CIA covertly conscripted around 50,000 of its men to fight in a “secret war” against the communist forces. After the war, when the Pathet Lao came to power, those who had served in these special guerrilla units were targeted with execution, imprisonment, and reeducation camps.

Among the men conscripted to fight on the US side of this “secret war” were the father and grandfather of the photographer Pao Houa Her. Her’s grandfather died in the conflict; her father survived, and, along with many others who served in the special guerrilla units, resolved to flee. Her was still a baby when her family escaped through the jungles of Laos, feeding her opium to keep her from crying and giving away their location, until they reached a refugee camp in Thailand. They eventually made their way to the Twin Cities, home to one of the largest communities of Hmong refugees in the US, in 1986.

Her’s work is rooted in her immigrant community’s enduring sense of displacement and loss. One of her photographic series, After the Fall of Hmong Teb Chaw (2017), was inspired by a case in which a Hmong man conned some four hundred Hmong elders, many of whom lived in the same senior center in St. Paul, out of $1.7 million. Loosely translated, teb chaw means “Hmong country” or “homeland”; the swindler told his victims that he was involved in establishing a new Hmong state in Southeast Asia and that their “investment” would guarantee them land there. So deep was their longing that many people, including some of the victims, contributed to the man’s legal fees after he was arrested.

Half of the images in After the Fall of Hmong Teb Chaw are black-and-white photographs taken inside the Como Park Conservatory in St. Paul, popular with Hmong locals, who are drawn to the warmth and the familiar tropical plants—transplants like themselves. The other half are portraits of elders engulfed in artificial foliage, a nod to the prevalence of fake flowers in traditional Hmong portraits. The conservatory photographs include glimpses of skylights and window frames—intentional clues that the backdrop is not actually a tropical location—and a plastic sheen or a light scattering of dust reveals the greenery to be fake. What the photographs evoke is not the homeland itself but the yearning for it.

The Imaginative Landscape is the fitting title of a new book that accompanied a pair of recent overlapping exhibitions of Her’s work at the John Michael Kohler Art Center in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, and the San José Museum of Art in California. It includes images from Attention, a series depicting men who served in the CIA’s special guerrilla units. These formal portraits of veterans in uniform, posing in three-quarter profile in front of luxurious red drapery, appear straightforward. In fact the men weren’t given US military uniforms or medals when they served; they either made the ones they’re wearing by hand or found them on eBay or in surplus stores. Nor were they ever recognized for their service or offered veterans’ benefits.

At the Kohler, the images were printed on ten large banners hung high above viewers’ heads, elevating the men literally and figuratively. Yet Her doesn’t name her subjects. Instead, each portrait bears the simple title of Hmong Veteran, because the men preferred to remain unidentified out of fear that they would be accused of “stolen valor”: it is a federal crime under US law to falsely claim military honors. “These men risked their lives for the United States,” Her says in an interview with the Kohler’s chief curator, Jodi Throckmorton, included in the book. “They’re trying to reinsert themselves into a history that they were very much a part of but have been all but forgotten.”

Advertisement

Her hadn’t been aware of the details of Hmong military service in the secret war until she attended an uncle’s funeral, where men in uniform played an unpolished version of “Taps” as they escorted his coffin, which was draped in an American flag—rituals she later learned they had taught themselves by watching YouTube videos. Her studied the historical paintings and photographs of famous generals and Civil War soldiers at the National Portrait Galleries in London and Washington, D.C., in order to incorporate their conventions, including the three-quarter profile, into her portraits.

Her is attuned to the cultural significance of portraiture—as a marker of status, or of affection. In another series she draws on elements of traditional Hmong portraiture to explore the fragmentation and displacement of families by the secret war. My grandmother’s favorite grandchild (2016–2018) consists of variations on a photograph Her inherited when her grandmother died, a studio portrait of a young child dressed in traditional, ornate Hmong attire and standing in front of a colorful scenic backdrop. Commissioned by Her’s grandmother in a refugee camp in Thailand before the family left for the US, it shows one of Her’s cousins—a cousin who wasn’t coming with them.

This photograph was the only image that her grandmother ever displayed of any of her grandchildren, and Her grew up seeing it whenever she visited. “There was always something really magical about it,” she told Audrey Sands in an interview that appears in her first book, the poignant My Grandfather Turned into a Tiger…and Other Illusions (2024). “She was always like this princess to me. It stood out as a thing that I would never be, but the thing that I could always aspire to be. I wanted to be my grandmother’s favorite grandchild.” After the portrait came into Her’s possession, she made copies of it and, in a sweetly furtive intervention,

Photoshopped versions with each of her cousins’ faces, as well as her own, transforming them all into their grandmother’s favorite grandchild.

During the recent exhibitions, Her’s work spilled out of the museums and into the surrounding neighborhoods as a kind of guerrilla art. In San Jose images were wheatpasted onto buildings and construction barriers, hung in a local restaurant, and slipped into a rotating electronic display announcing events at the convention center. In Sheboygan they could be found on an illuminated sign on the grounds of 3 Sheeps Brewing, on a billboard at the Kohler Art Preserve (a ten-minute drive down the highway from the museum), on the walls of the Hmong Mutual Assistance Association, and at the Sheboygan County Circuit Court, where pictures of Hmong elders from her Imaginative Landscape series kept company with the portraits of robed judges, all white men.

Her wants her work to be visible to people going about their daily lives who may or may not find their way into a museum, just as she wants to challenge museumgoers. Her engrossing wall-sized videos of kwv txhiaj, or traditional song poetry, for instance, are entirely in Hmong (though visitors to both museums could scan a QR code for the English translations). “I love that there is a language, whether the language of photography or just the language of looking, that not everybody understands, or not everybody is privy to the notion of image-making,” Her told Paul Schmelzer in a 2022 interview. “I like that it reads so differently in different communities.”

Her’s use of vernacular materials, from wheatpasted posters or lawn signs to lenticular photography—made with special lenses to produce an illusion of depth—is both an invitation to viewers outside of the art world and a broadening of the conventions of museum display. The photographs that make up her series Pictures of paradise (2022–2024), for example, change when viewed from different angles. The form is more typically used for advertisements or novelty items like magnets or postcards, but Her used it to make large-scale images of the Laotian jungle after a 2022 trip with her family during which her father showed them the places where they had lived while fleeing.

As Lauren Schell Dickens, a senior curator at the San José Museum, points out in an essay in The Imaginative Landscape, Her’s Pictures of paradise is, in part, a response to Thomas Struth’s 1998 Paradise series. His photographs are of jungles or forests from around the world that he imagined were unaltered by human intervention. But Her’s present the jungle as a place where children were born, couples married, and people became ill and died. Viewed in person, the photographs are disorienting and hypnotic. Aspects of the landscape come in and out of focus, as though sunlight were filtering through branches or breezes were ruffling the leaves. The lenticular format seems to fold the reality of Laos into Her’s “memories” of Laos—memories handed down from her grandmother, who came over every weekend and told her stories about jungle spirits, and from her father, who worked at night and recorded folktales for Her and her sister to listen to on cassettes as they went to sleep.

Advertisement

At times Her’s work brings to mind that of An-My Lê, who was evacuated with her family from Saigon by the US military in 1975, when she was about fifteen. Lê’s large-scale photographs of tangled branches and dense sections of jungle in her series Viêt Nam (1994–1998), made on her first return trip, are given a formal elegance by their flawless black-and-white printing. But both Lê and Her combine fact and fiction. In her series Small Wars (1999–2002), Lê photographed—and sometimes participated in—the restaging of battles from the Vietnam War by reenactors in rural Virginia and North Carolina, who planted bamboo to replicate the vegetation of Vietnam in woods otherwise populated by the pine, spruce, and kudzu of the American South. Commenting on the paradoxical nature of landscape photography in an essay last year, Lê pointed to “its capacity to render the present in searing detail, while also evoking both the past and future through subjective suggestion.”

The past and the present for the Hmong American community intermingle in Her’s latest series, Seeds of History, recently on view at the Kohler. She made black-and-white photographs of Hmong residents of Sheboygan, out of doors, with the large leafy trees of Wisconsin behind them and a dense field of opium poppies in the foreground. For Hmong people poppies are symbols of prosperity, recalling a time when they cultivated the plant in Laos. “Elders often reflect on those days of prosperity,” Her writes in The Imaginative Landscape, “as a time when the land held more than just crops, but a sense of hope.”

That hope, and that history, is what has drawn many Hmong people to the Mount Shasta region of Northern California during the past two decades to become marijuana farmers. Her traveled to the region a few years ago to make a series of black-and-white landscape photographs. The mountainous, rocky terrain recalls northern Laos, where Hmong farmers grew poppies for generations; here, as there, they must carry in the water needed to coax a crop out of unfavorable soil.

Unlike many of Her’s other photographs, her Mt. Shasta series (2021–2022) contains no people. Instead it shows dry, twisted tree branches and yellowed grasses, sometimes with the white mountain peaks in the distance. But the images include evidence of humans, and of the labor that goes into growing a crop in such an inhospitable landscape: a serpentine hose, a plastic bag caught on a branch, a piece of discarded netting. Her mounts the photographs on lightboxes, borrowing a format most often used for advertising to suggest the glow of the American Dream—even as the idea is instantly undercut by the hardscrabble emptiness of the landscapes.

In Her’s work, imagined landscapes often resonate more than real ones. The flowers in her portraits are no less treasured for being made of plastic; the military uniforms worn by the Hmong veterans command respect despite being cobbled together by the veterans themselves. She and her cousins are her grandmother’s favorites because Her created and “documented” that imagined reality, photographing it into being.
